The temperature these are usually served.Popsicle from the freezer: Legend says 11-year-old Frank Epperson invented it in 1905 by leaving soda and a stirring stick outside on a freezing night.
The temperature these are usually served.Scooped ice cream: It's served warmer than the freezer, around -12°C, because ice cream that's too cold numbs your tongue and mutes the flavour.
The temperature these are usually served.Cold lager: 'Lager' is German for 'storage': these beers were aged cold in caves, and the cool fermentation gives a crisp, clean taste.
The temperature these are usually served.White wine: Serving it too cold mutes its aromas, which is why a slightly chilled glass lets the fruit and floral notes show.
The temperature these are usually served.Red wine: 'Room temperature' for red wine dates from chilly European castles, not modern heated homes, so cellar-cool is better.
The temperature these are usually served.Warm sake: Called kan in Japanese, warm sake is a winter tradition and also helps mask rougher cheap brews.
The temperature these are usually served.Cappuccino milk: Steaming milk past about 65°C starts to make it taste flat, and well past that it can scald.
The temperature these are usually served.Fresh black coffee: Coffee is brewed around 90 to 96°C, but sipping it at 80°C will burn your mouth, so it needs to cool first.
The temperature these are usually served.Water for black tea: Black tea wants water just off the boil, while delicate green tea prefers it noticeably cooler.
The temperature these are usually served.Oil for fondue bourguignonne: Fondue bourguignonne has diners cook cubes of beef at the table in hot oil, a different dish from Swiss cheese fondue.

Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.Thespis: Their first collaboration, though most of its music is lost, and only one song survives.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.Trial by Jury: A one-act comedy set entirely in a courtroom, sung from start to finish with no spoken dialogue.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.The Sorcerer: Their first full-length hit, with a love potion that makes everyone in a village fall for the wrong person.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.H.M.S. Pinafore: Their first international smash, mocking the Navy's rulers, including the song 'I Am the Monarch of the Sea' in the first lord's honour.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.The Pirates of Penzance: Premiered in New York on 31 December 1879 to secure US copyright, and it contains 'the very model of a modern major-general'.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.Patience: A satire of the aesthetic movement, with a poet character often seen as parodying Oscar Wilde, who was sent on a US tour to promote it.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.Iolanthe: Pits fairies against the House of Lords, and a lord chancellor sings a famous patter song.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.The Mikado: Set in fictional Japan, it was a hit during a London craze for Japanese style and ran for 672 performances.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.The Yeomen of the Guard: Their most serious work, set at the Tower of London, with a bittersweet ending.
Gilbert and Sullivan operettas, by premi.The Gondoliers: Set in Venice, it was their last big hit, and soon after came the 'carpet quarrel' that broke up the partnership.

Black holes by mass.Gaia BH1: Found in 2022 about 1,500 light-years away, it was the closest known black hole at discovery, orbiting a Sun-like star.
Black holes by mass.Cygnus X-1: Discovered as an X-ray source in 1964, it was among the first black hole candidates; Stephen Hawking bet against it and lost.
Black holes by mass.Gaia BH3: Spotted in 2024 about 2,000 light-years away through the wobble of its companion star, it is the heaviest stellar black hole in our galaxy.
Black holes by mass.GW150914 merger result: This was the first gravitational-wave detection, by LIGO in 2015: two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light-years away.
Black holes by mass.GW190521 merger result: Two black holes merged to form one of the first confirmed intermediate-mass black holes, a size once thought to be rare or missing.
Black holes by mass.Sagittarius A*: The black hole at the center of our Milky Way, about 26,000 light-years away; its first image came in 2022 and its study earned a 2020 Nobel Prize.
Black holes by mass.Andromeda's central hole: Our neighboring galaxy is on a course to collide with the Milky Way in several billion years, so its central black hole may one day meet ours.
Black holes by mass.Sombrero Galaxy's hole: This galaxy takes its name from its bright bulge and dark dust lane, which together look like a wide-brimmed hat, and lies about 30 million light-years away.
Black holes by mass.M87*: In 2019 it became the first black hole ever photographed, as a glowing ring captured by the Event Horizon Telescope.
Black holes by mass.TON 618: It powers a quasar so luminous that the light we see left it over ten billion years ago; its mass is among the biggest ever measured.

Land speed record cars, by record speed.La Jamais Contente (1899): Camille Jenatzy's electric car, shaped like a torpedo, was the first car to pass 100 km/h.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.Stanley Rocket (1906): A steam car set this record at Daytona, and steam cars soon lost their record-setting crown.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.Sunbeam 1000 HP (1927): It was the first car to top 200 mph, powered by a huge aircraft engine and driven by Henry Segrave.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.Golden Arrow (1929): Segrave returned to break the record again at Daytona, but died the following year in a speedboat record attempt.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.Campbell's Blue Bird (1935): Malcolm Campbell took the first car above 300 mph on the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.Railton Mobil Special (1947): John Cobb set this on Bonneville's salt flats, and died in 1952 trying to break a water speed record on Loch Ness.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.Bluebird-Proteus CN7 (1964): Donald Campbell set it in Australia on Lake Eyre; it was the last wheel-driven land speed record.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.The Blue Flame (1970): Gary Gabelich's rocket-powered car burned liquefied natural gas and hydrogen peroxide and was the first to pass 600 mph.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.Thrust2 (1983): Richard Noble's jet car set this in Nevada's Black Rock Desert, and he later led the Thrust SSC project.
Land speed record cars, by record speed.Thrust SSC (1997): Andy Green drove it faster than sound in the Nevada desert in 1997, the first supersonic land speed record.

Horsepower of famous cars.Benz Patent-Motorwagen: Karl Benz's 1886 three-wheeler is widely seen as the first practical car; his wife Bertha made the first long road trip in one in 1888.
Horsepower of famous cars.Citroën 2CV (1948): Citroën's brief asked for a car that could carry two farmers in clogs and a basket of eggs across a ploughed field without breaking any.
Horsepower of famous cars.Ford Model T: Henry Ford's moving assembly line cut its build time from over twelve hours to about ninety minutes; more than 15 million were made.
Horsepower of famous cars.Classic Mini (1959): Alec Issigonis turned the engine sideways to save space, so about 80 percent of the little car's floor plan was left for people and luggage.
Horsepower of famous cars.Jaguar E-Type (3.8): After its 1961 Geneva debut, Enzo Ferrari reportedly called it the most beautiful car ever made.
Horsepower of famous cars.Lamborghini Countach LP400: Its name is a Piedmontese exclamation of astonishment, and its upward-swinging scissor doors became a Lamborghini signature.
Horsepower of famous cars.Ferrari F40: Built to celebrate Ferrari's 40th anniversary, it was the last car Enzo Ferrari approved before his death in 1988, and it came with twin turbos.
Horsepower of famous cars.McLaren F1: It seats the driver in the middle with a passenger on each side, and in 1998 it set a production-car speed record of 240 mph that stood for years.
Horsepower of famous cars.Bugatti Veyron: Its 16-cylinder engine was built to push the car past 400 km/h; Bugatti reportedly lost money on every one it sold.
Horsepower of famous cars.Bugatti Chiron: Named for Monégasque racing driver Louis Chiron, its 8.0 litre W16 engine is fed by four turbochargers.

When these famous grounds opened.Lord's (current site): Thomas Lord founded it, and it is the home of cricket; the current site, the third Lord's, opened in 1814 near Regent's Park.
When these famous grounds opened.Melbourne Cricket Ground: It hosted the first Test match in 1877 between Australia and England, and it hosted the 1956 Olympics.
When these famous grounds opened.Anfield: Anfield was originally Everton's home before an argument over rent in 1892 led to the founding of Liverpool FC.
When these famous grounds opened.Old Trafford: Bobby Charlton nicknamed it the Theatre of Dreams, and it was rebuilt after wartime bomb damage in the 1940s.
When these famous grounds opened.Fenway Park: The oldest ballpark still in use in Major League Baseball, it has a 37-foot left field wall called the Green Monster.
When these famous grounds opened.Wrigley Field: The ivy on its outfield walls is famous, and Wrigley Field had no lights for night games until 1988.
When these famous grounds opened.Santiago Bernabeu: Real Madrid's home is named after its longtime president Santiago Bernabeu, who led the club for 35 years.
When these famous grounds opened.Maracana: Built for the 1950 World Cup, it hosted the final with nearly 200,000 people present, a record crowd.
When these famous grounds opened.Camp Nou: Barcelona's stadium, the name means new field in Catalan, and it is the biggest stadium in Europe.
When these famous grounds opened.Allianz Arena: Its exterior panels can glow red, blue or white depending on which team is playing, and it is Munich's home.

More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Joseph: Joseph's lifespan shows him as the youngest of this group, and he rose from slavery to become a powerful official in Egypt.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Aaron: Aaron was Moses' brother and the first high priest of Israel, and he died on Mount Hor.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Sarah: Sarah is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is recorded, and she bore Isaac when she was about 90.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Jacob: Jacob was also called Israel, and his twelve sons became the tribes of Israel.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Isaac: Isaac was the son of Abraham, and he was nearly sacrificed, and he lived to see his sons grow old.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Enoch: Enoch is described as walking with God and being taken, and he lived far less long than his peers, and Genesis says he did not die.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Arpachshad: Arpachshad was a descendant of Noah's son Shem, and he was born two years after the flood.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Enosh: Enosh was the son of Seth, and Genesis says it was in his time that people began to call on the name of the Lord.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Seth: Seth was Adam and Eve's third son, born after Abel's death, and he is regarded as an ancestor of Noah.
More biblical lifespans, from Genesis on.Jared: Jared was the father of Enoch, and his 962 years are the third longest on record, after Methuselah and Jared sits below.

Players per side on the field of play.Beach volleyball: Played on sand, this duo format became an Olympic sport in 1996, and the players tell each other the serve with hidden hand signals behind their backs.
Players per side on the field of play.Polo: Riders switch ponies between periods called chukkers, since the horses tire quickly, and a top player may use several in a single match.
Players per side on the field of play.Basketball: James Naismith's 1891 original had nine players per side and peach baskets, and the five-player format came a little later, with the baskets cut open.
Players per side on the field of play.Ice hockey: A slap shot with the puck can top 160 km/h, and players change lines in shifts of a minute or so, since skating at full speed is exhausting.
Players per side on the field of play.Netball: Evolved from women's basketball in the late 19th century, this game restricts each player to certain areas of the court, so nobody can run with the ball.
Players per side on the field of play.Baseball: Baseball's nine fielders include the catcher, who flashes secret finger signs to the pitcher before every delivery.
Players per side on the field of play.Men's field lacrosse: This game of Native American origin was once played by hundreds of people over miles of land, and some tribes called it 'little brother of war'.
Players per side on the field of play.Soccer: The Cambridge Rules of 1848 were an early attempt to write down this game, and many modern rules trace back to the 1863 Football Association.
Players per side on the field of play.Rugby union: Rugby School in England gave the game its name, and legend says William Webb Ellis first picked up the ball and ran with it in 1823.
Players per side on the field of play.Australian rules football: A kick between the two tall central posts scores six points, while one between a tall and a short post scores just one.

Famous poems, by number of lines.Bashō's frog haiku: The seventeen-syllable verse by Matsuo Bashō about a frog jumping into an old pond is the most famous haiku in Japan.
Dylan Thomas wrote this villanelle for his dying father, and its repeated lines urge him to 'rage, rage against the dying of the light'.
Famous poems, by number of lines.Kubla Khan: Coleridge said an opium dream inspired this poem, and a visitor from Porlock interrupted him as he wrote it, leaving it unfinished.
Famous poems, by number of lines.The Raven: Poe's poem of a grieving man and a talking bird got him famous, but little money, only about 9 dollars at the time of its publication.
Famous poems, by number of lines.The Waste Land: T. S. Eliot's modernist masterpiece includes the opening 'April is the cruellest month', and Ezra Pound heavily edited it.
Famous poems, by number of lines.Beowulf: This Old English epic about a hero who fights a monster Grendel survives in a single manuscript, which was damaged in a 1731 fire.
Famous poems, by number of lines.Paradise Lost: Milton wrote this epic about the fall of Satan and Adam and Eve, and he was blind and dictated it to assistants.
Famous poems, by number of lines.The Odyssey: Homer's epic about Odysseus' 10-year voyage home from Troy gave us the word 'odyssey', and its hero is also known for the Trojan horse.
Famous poems, by number of lines.The Iliad: Homer's poem about the Trojan War takes place over a few weeks, and it opens with the rage of Achilles.
Famous poems, by number of lines.The Mahabharata: This Sanskrit epic is about 10 times the length of the Iliad and Odyssey combined, and it includes the Bhagavad Gita.

Ancient sites, from west to east.Chichén Itzá: Chichén Itzá, a Maya city in Yucatán, has a pyramid whose staircases are aligned so that the equinox shadows form a serpent descending.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Machu Picchu: Machu Picchu, an Inca citadel built in the 15th century, remained unknown to the outside world until Hiram Bingham publicized it in 1911.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Stonehenge: Stonehenge's giant stones were erected around 2500 BC, and the smaller bluestones were hauled about 150 miles from Wales.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Carthage: Carthage, founded by Phoenicians, was Rome's great rival, and after the Punic Wars Rome razed it in 146 BC.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Petra: Petra, the 'rose-red city' carved from sandstone, was the capital of the Nabataeans, who grew rich as traders in incense and spices.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Persepolis: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire, and it was burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BC.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Mohenjo-daro: Mohenjo-daro, in modern Pakistan, was a city of the Indus Valley civilization with drains and a grid layout over 4,000 years ago.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Angkor Wat: Angkor Wat, built in the 12th century as a Hindu temple, is the largest religious monument in the world and appears on Cambodia's flag.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Terracotta Army, Xi'an: The Terracotta Army, found by farmers digging a well in 1974, includes thousands of life-size soldiers guarding the first emperor of China.
Ancient sites, from west to east.Tōdai-ji, Nara: Tōdai-ji houses one of the world's largest bronze Buddha statues, in what is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world.

Voltages around the house.AA battery: The 1.5 V comes from alkaline chemistry, not size; AAA, AA and D cells all give 1.5 V, but a D lasts far longer.
Voltages around the house.Phone lithium-ion cell: A lithium-ion cell sits at about 3.7 V nominally, and phones include protection circuits because overcharging one can start a fire.
Voltages around the house.USB port: USB's 5 V suits the logic chips it was designed for, though modern USB-C Power Delivery can go up to 48 V.
Voltages around the house.Smoke-alarm battery: The rectangular 9 V battery is secretly six small 1.5-volt cells stacked together inside the case.
Voltages around the house.Car battery: A lead-acid car battery has six cells of about 2.1 V each, so a full charge reads nearer 12.6 V.
Voltages around the house.Landline phone (idle): Old phone lines idle at around 48 V DC, with a stronger AC signal of around 90 V sent down the line to make it ring.
Voltages around the house.US wall outlet: America settled near the 110 V that Edison's early power stations supplied, and its outlets are now rated at 120 V.
Voltages around the house.UK wall outlet: Britain moved from 240 V to a European-wide 230 V standard in the 1990s, though real supply barely changed.
Voltages around the house.Electric fence pulse: A fence pulses thousands of volts in short bursts with a tiny current, which stings animals without being dangerous.
Voltages around the house.Car spark plug: A coil steps the 12-volt battery up to 25,000 V or more so a spark can leap the gap and ignite the fuel.

Song running times (album versions).Song 2 (Blur): The 'woo-hoo' chant was a joke by Blur about grunge bands, but it became their biggest US hit.
Song running times (album versions).Wannabe (Spice Girls): The Spice Girls' debut single hit number one in more than 30 countries, and its video was shot in a single continuous take.
Song running times (album versions).Imagine (John Lennon): Lennon recorded it in 1971 at his home studio at Tittenhurst Park, with Phil Spector co-producing.
Song running times (album versions).Africa (Toto): David Paich wrote it though no one in Toto had been to Africa; it has had a huge revival through memes.
Song running times (album versions).Bohemian Rhapsody: Record company bosses said it was too long for radio, but DJ Kenny Everett played it and it stayed number one in the UK for nine weeks.
Song running times (album versions).Hey Jude: Written to comfort Julian Lennon, it was then the longest number one single in UK chart history, with a coda of four minutes.
Song running times (album versions).Stairway to Heaven: It was never released as a single in the US yet became one of the most played radio songs.
Song running times (album versions).Free Bird: Fans shouting its title at unrelated concerts became a running joke, but the song itself is a long guitar epic.
Song running times (album versions).The End (The Doors): Its spoken section appears in the opening of Apocalypse Now, which made the song newly infamous.
Song running times (album versions).In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida: Legend says the title is a drunken slur of 'In the Garden of Eden', and the long version filled a whole LP side.

The year each story is set in.Titanic (film): The 'unsinkable' liner struck an iceberg and over 1,500 died; James Cameron's film won 11 Oscars.
The year each story is set in.The Great Gatsby: Fitzgerald's Jazz Age novel sold modestly in his lifetime and became a classic only after World War II.
The year each story is set in.Casablanca: Set in Vichy-era Morocco but filmed on a Hollywood lot, it won the Best Picture Oscar.
The year each story is set in.Dirty Dancing: Set at a Catskills resort in 1963, its song '(I've Had) The Time of My Life' won an Oscar.
The year each story is set in.Apollo 13 (film): The film changed the real line to 'Houston, we have a problem'; the astronauts actually said 'we've had a problem'.
The year each story is set in.Stranger Things, season 1: Set in fictional Hawkins, Indiana, it was the Duffer brothers' show that revived 1980s nostalgia.
The year each story is set in.Independence Day (film): Its scene of aliens blasting the White House became one of the most memorable in disaster movies.
The year each story is set in.Back to the Future II's future: The sequel predicted hoverboards, flying cars and the Chicago Cubs winning the World Series, which the Cubs did in 2016.
The year each story is set in.Blade Runner (original): Set in Los Angeles, it was based on Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
The year each story is set in.Children of Men: Alfonso Cuarón's film, based on a P. D. James novel, imagines a world where no babies are born, and features long unbroken takes.

Sports balls by diameter.Table tennis ball: The standard grew from 38 to 40 mm in 2000, partly to slow the game down and make it easier for TV viewers to follow.
Sports balls by diameter.Golf ball: Its dimples, usually several hundred, cut drag and add lift, letting a golf ball fly much farther than a smooth one.
Sports balls by diameter.Snooker ball: A frame starts with 22 balls: 15 reds, six colours and a white cue ball; the maximum break is 147.
Sports balls by diameter.Pool ball: Pool balls are typically a tough phenolic resin; for centuries, billiard balls were carved from ivory.
Sports balls by diameter.Tennis ball: Tennis balls turned yellow in 1972 to be easier to see on TV; Wimbledon held out until 1986.
Sports balls by diameter.Baseball: A regulation ball has 108 raised red stitches, all sewn by hand.
Sports balls by diameter.Softball: Despite its name, it is hard; the game began in Chicago in 1887, reportedly first played with a boxing glove for a ball.
Sports balls by diameter.Men's handball: Players rub sticky resin on their hands to grip it, and shots in this fast game can exceed 100 km/h.
Sports balls by diameter.Soccer ball (size 5): The classic 32-panel design was made famous by Adidas's Telstar at the 1970 World Cup.
Sports balls by diameter.Basketball (size 7): Women's games use a slightly smaller ball, size 6, while the men's ball is this size.

When these breakfast cereals launched.Shredded Wheat: Shredded Wheat was one of the first breakfast cereals, and it was invented in Colorado as a health food, partly inspired by a dyspeptic patient.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Grape-Nuts: Despite its name, it has neither grapes nor nuts. Its flavour comes from the malted barley and its nutty taste, and its tough crunch is famous.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Bircher muesli: Swiss doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner created it for hospital patients, mixing oats, apples and nuts, and it is still a Swiss breakfast staple.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Wheaties: Billed as the 'Breakfast of Champions', it began as an accidental spill of bran gruel on a hot stove, and it was advertised on a baseball broadcast.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Rice Krispies: The snap, crackle and pop in its ads came from the sound of the rice puffs in milk, and the elves were drawn to promote it.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Cheerios: General Mills first sold it as CheeriOats, and it is still the best-selling brand of the company.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Frosted Flakes: Tony the Tiger and his 'They're Gr-r-reat!' catchphrase helped make this sugar-coated flake a hit, and it was first called Sugar Frosted Flakes.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Lucky Charms: Its marshmallow shapes were added as an experiment by a General Mills employee who mixed Lucky Charms bits from candy and cereal.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Honey Nut Cheerios: It added honey and almond flavour to the original oat ring cereal and it has become one of the best-selling cereals in the U.S.
When these breakfast cereals launched.Cinnamon Toast Crunch: The swirled squares were made to taste like a sweet, spicy pastry, and its fans call the cereal's extra-sugary milk the best part.

The fall of Rome, step by step.Crisis of the Third Century: In about fifty years more than twenty emperors came and went, most murdered or killed in battle, while plague, invasion and inflation hit.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Persians capture Valerian: Persian king Shapur I captured Valerian, the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner by an enemy, and he died in captivity.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Aurelian walls in Rome: The Aurelian Walls, about 19 km long, still stand in much of Rome, a sign that the city now needed defending.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Diocletian's Tetrarchy: Diocletian split rule among four men, two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars, because one ruler couldn't manage the vast empire alone.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Edict of Milan: Constantine and Licinius's edict granted religious freedom across the empire, ending official persecution of Christians.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Disaster at Adrianople: At Adrianople, Gothic horsemen crushed a Roman army and killed Emperor Valens, showing that legions could be beaten by barbarians.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Empire splits for good: When Theodosius I died, his sons inherited West and East; the Eastern half, later called Byzantine, lasted over a thousand years more.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Visigoths sack Rome: Alaric's Visigoths looted Rome for three days, the first time in about 800 years that the city had fallen to a foreign enemy.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Vandals sack Rome: The Vandals plundered Rome for two weeks under King Genseric, and the word vandalism comes from their name.
The fall of Rome, step by step.Last western emperor deposed: Odoacer removed Romulus Augustulus, a teenage boy whose name combined Rome's founder Romulus and its first emperor Augustus.

Developer tools by first release.Emacs: Richard Stallman's extensible editor is customized with a Lisp dialect, and sparked decades of friendly 'editor wars' with vi.
Developer tools by first release.Vim: An improved version of vi by Bram Moolenaar, whose modal editing is famously hard for newcomers to quit.
Developer tools by first release.Eclipse: IBM built it for Java and then released it as open source; it was the dominant Java IDE for years.
Developer tools by first release.Git: Linus Torvalds wrote it within weeks after the Linux kernel lost access to its previous version-control tool.
Developer tools by first release.GitHub: Built around Git, the hosting site was bought by Microsoft in 2018 for about 7.5 billion dollars.
Developer tools by first release.npm: Node's package manager now hosts millions of packages, and in 2016 the removal of tiny 'left-pad' broke many builds.
Developer tools by first release.Docker: It popularized containers, which bundle an app with everything it needs so it runs the same everywhere.
Developer tools by first release.Kubernetes: Google open-sourced it from its internal Borg system; the name is Greek for 'helmsman', and K8s is its shorthand.
Developer tools by first release.VS Code: Microsoft's free editor, built on web technology, became the most popular code editor in developer surveys.
Developer tools by first release.GitHub Copilot: Powered by OpenAI models, it suggests code as you type and was among the first mainstream AI coding assistants.

South American countries by area.Suriname: The smallest country on the continent, it is covered mostly by rainforest, with most people on the coast.
South American countries by area.Guyana: The only English-speaking country in South America, it is home to Kaieteur Falls, a huge single-drop waterfall.
South American countries by area.Ecuador: It is named for the equator, and includes the Galápagos Islands that helped inspire Darwin.
South American countries by area.Paraguay: Landlocked, with Guaraní, an indigenous language, widely spoken alongside Spanish by most of the population.
South American countries by area.Chile: About 4,300 km long yet averaging under 200 km wide, it is one of the longest, thinnest countries.
South American countries by area.Venezuela: Home to Angel Falls, at 979 m the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, and vast oil reserves.
South American countries by area.Colombia: The only South American country with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.
South American countries by area.Peru: Home of Machu Picchu and the Nazca Lines, and potatoes originated in the Andes near Lake Titicaca.
South American countries by area.Argentina: It has Aconcagua, the tallest peak outside Asia, rising to about 6,960 m in the Andes.
South American countries by area.Brazil: Covers about half of South America and is the only Portuguese-speaking country on the continent.

When these Chinese dynasties began.Xia: The first dynasty in Chinese tradition, its legendary founder Yu the Great is said to have tamed floods, though archaeologists still debate whether it existed.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Shang: Its kings wrote questions to ancestors on animal bones and turtle shells, the earliest known Chinese writing.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Zhou: It lasted roughly 800 years, the longest of any Chinese dynasty, and Confucius lived during its later decline.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Qin: China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, was buried with a Terracotta Army, yet the dynasty lasted only about 15 years.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Han: It gave its name to the Han Chinese majority, and it opened the Silk Road and saw paper invented.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Sui: It built the Grand Canal linking north and south, but it collapsed within about 40 years.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Tang: Its capital Chang'an was among the largest cities in the world, and the era is considered a golden age of poetry.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Song: Printing, gunpowder weapons and the first government paper money flourished under it, and its seafarers used the compass.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Yuan: Founded by Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, this Mongol-ruled dynasty hosted the traveler Marco Polo, according to his account.
When these Chinese dynasties began.Ming: It built much of the Great Wall as it stands now, and the Forbidden City in Beijing, and sent admiral Zheng He's treasure fleets abroad.

Household liquids by pH.Battery acid: Lead-acid car batteries use sulfuric acid, which is strong enough to burn skin.
Household liquids by pH.Lemon juice: Its sour taste is from citric acid, and a few drops can keep sliced apples from browning.
Household liquids by pH.Tomato juice: Its acidity is why ketchup and canned tomatoes need careful canning, and it makes a good marinade.
Household liquids by pH.Black coffee: Roasting makes coffee mildly acidic, and cold brew tends to taste smoother because it extracts fewer of the sharp-tasting acids.
Household liquids by pH.Pure water: At exactly 7 it is neutral, as in distilled water at room temperature, and rain is naturally slightly acidic.
Household liquids by pH.Baking soda solution: Sodium bicarbonate is mildly alkaline, which is why it neutralizes acid and works as an antacid and deodorizer.
Household liquids by pH.Milk of magnesia: A suspension of magnesium hydroxide, used as an antacid and laxative.
Household liquids by pH.Household ammonia: Ammonia is a gas dissolved in water, and its sharp smell comes from the escaping gas.
Household liquids by pH.Bleach: Bleach is strongly alkaline, and mixing it with ammonia or acids can release toxic gases.
Household liquids by pH.Drain cleaner: Drain cleaners contain lye, which turns grease into soap, and it can burn skin.

Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.A shooting star's streak: Most meteors are grains of dust, often smaller than a pebble, burning up around 100 km above us as they hit the atmosphere at tremendous speed.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.Longest total solar eclipse: The Moon's shadow on Earth is only a few hundred kilometres wide, so totality races across the ground and rarely lasts more than a few minutes.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.Longest total lunar eclipse: The Moon turns coppery red because sunlight bends through Earth's atmosphere; it is effectively lit by every sunrise and sunset at once.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.One Earth day: A day measured against the stars is about four minutes shorter, at around 23 hours 56 minutes, and Earth's spin is slowly lengthening it.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.Moon's cycle of phases: The Moon takes about 27.3 days to circle Earth, but the cycle of phases is longer because Earth also moves around the Sun.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.Gap between Mars oppositions: Mars is brightest at opposition, and spacecraft launch windows to the planet open on roughly the same schedule.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.Sunspot cycle: Heinrich Schwabe discovered this in 1843 after years of watching the Sun for a planet inside Mercury's orbit.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.Saros eclipse cycle: The Babylonians likely knew it; the name comes from Edmond Halley, and it lets eclipses be predicted almost like clockwork.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.Wobble of Earth's axis: Earth's axis traces a slow circle, so in about 12,000 years Vega, not Polaris, will serve as our pole star.
Cosmic clocks: how long each lasts.Sun's hydrogen-burning life: The Sun is only about halfway through that span, roughly 4.6 billion years old, before it swells into a red giant.

One hit single for each year of the 1980.Another One Bites the Dust: John Deacon wrote its bass line, and Michael Jackson urged Queen to release it as a single.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.Tainted Love (Soft Cell): Soft Cell's synth cover of a 1964 soul song by Gloria Jones set a record for time on the US Hot 100.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.Eye of the Tiger: Survivor wrote it after Sylvester Stallone asked for a theme for Rocky III, and it won a Grammy.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.Every Breath You Take: Sting wrote it during his marriage breakdown; the stalker-like lyric is often mistaken for a love song.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.When Doves Cry: Prince's hit famously has no bass line, and it came from the film Purple Rain.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.We Are the World: Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie wrote it, and over 40 stars recorded it in one night for African famine relief.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.Livin' on a Prayer: Its talk-box guitar and mid-song key change became stadium singalong staples.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.Never Gonna Give You Up: Rick Astley's hit became the Rickroll, a prank meme that took off in 2007.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.Fast Car (Tracy Chapman): Luke Combs's 2023 cover brought this folk-rock story of escape back to the country charts.
One hit single for each year of the 1980.Like a Prayer: Madonna's video with burning crosses led Pepsi to cancel its sponsorship deal with her.

Milestones in the history of wine.Dom Pérignon joins Hautvillers: Tradition credits Dom Pérignon, a monk, with perfecting sparkling wine. In reality he worked mostly to keep bubbles out of the wine.
Milestones in the history of wine.Tokaj vineyards classified: Hungary's Tokaj region set up one of the world's first classified wine regions. Its sweet Tokaji was called the wine of kings.
Milestones in the history of wine.Riddling table invented: The riddling table, or pupitre, let Champagne houses turn bottles gradually to collect sediment. This made clear sparkling wine practical.
Milestones in the history of wine.Bordeaux classification: Napoleon III requested this ranking for the 1855 Paris Exposition. Remarkably, it has only been changed once, when Mouton was promoted.
Milestones in the history of wine.Phylloxera reaches France: The tiny aphid phylloxera, arriving from America, destroyed most European vines. The fix was grafting vines onto American roots.
Milestones in the history of wine.France creates the AOC system: AOC rules say where and how a wine may be made. They started in France and became the model for protected origin labels worldwide.
Milestones in the history of wine.Robert Mondavi Winery opens: Mondavi helped put Napa Valley on the world wine map. He was a leading champion of California wines in the 1960s and beyond.
Milestones in the history of wine.Mouton Rothschild promoted: Château Mouton Rothschild was upgraded to a first growth in 1973 after decades of lobbying. Its labels feature art by famous painters.
Milestones in the history of wine.The Judgment of Paris: At a blind tasting in Paris, French judges ranked California wines above top French ones. The result stunned the wine world.
Milestones in the history of wine.Two Buck Chuck launches: Trader Joe's Charles Shaw wine sold for $1.99 at first in California. It became a cult hit and sold hundreds of millions of bottles.

Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Canadian dime: The Canadian dime is the smallest silver-colored coin in Canada, and its tiny size has made it notable among world currency.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Australian 5 cents: Australia's 5 cent coin features an echidna and is the smallest coin in circulation there.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Australian $2: The Australian $2 coin is gold-colored, features an Aboriginal elder and is smaller than the $1 coin, which surprises tourists.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Canadian nickel: The Canadian nickel shows a beaver, and it's made largely of steel with nickel plating today.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Japanese 5 yen: The Japanese 5 yen coin has a hole in the middle and is brass, and it's seen as lucky since its pronunciation 'go-en' means good fortune.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Canadian quarter: The Canadian quarter has had many commemorative designs, including a caribou on the standard version.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Australian $1: The Australian $1 coin shows five kangaroos and has a distinctive twelve-sided shape, which helps blind users tell it apart.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Canadian loonie: Canada's loonie got its nickname from the loon on its back, and it was introduced in 1987 to replace the paper bill.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Canadian toonie: The toonie is a two-tone coin with a polar bear on the back, and its name is a play on loonie and two.
Canadian, Australian and Japanese coins.Australian 50 cents: The Australian 50 cent coin is a large twelve-sided piece, and it's one of the biggest coins in circulation worldwide.

When these condiment brands began.Grey Poupon: Named for Dijon's mustard-makers Grey and Poupon. Its 1970s ads had a man in a Rolls-Royce asking 'Pardon me, do you have any Grey Poupon?'
When these condiment brands began.Tabasco: Edmund McIlhenny started it on Louisiana's Avery Island, where it is still made and the peppers are aged in oak barrels.
When these condiment brands began.Maggi seasoning: Swiss miller Julius Maggi created the liquid seasoning to make nutritious soups for working families. It is now a kitchen staple across continents.
When these condiment brands began.Marmite: A by-product of beer brewing, since it is made from leftover yeast. Its 'love it or hate it' slogan dates from 1996.
When these condiment brands began.French's mustard: The bright, mild yellow mustard is popularly linked to hot dogs at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair.
When these condiment brands began.Hellmann's mayonnaise: Richard Hellmann's New York deli sold it first. West of the Rockies the same recipe was branded Best Foods.
When these condiment brands began.Vegemite: Created in Melbourne as an Australian answer to Marmite, using leftover brewer's yeast.
When these condiment brands began.Kewpie mayonnaise: Japan's rich mayo uses only egg yolks, and takes its name from the Kewpie doll on the jar.
When these condiment brands began.Miracle Whip: Kraft launched it at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair as a cheaper, sweeter option for Depression-era households.
When these condiment brands began.Huy Fong Sriracha: Vietnamese refugee David Tran founded it in Los Angeles. Its rooster logo reflects his birth year in the Chinese zodiac.

Human spaceflights by duration.Shepard's Freedom 7: Alan Shepard's suborbital hop made him the first American in space. A decade later he walked on the Moon on Apollo 14.
Human spaceflights by duration.Gagarin's Vostok 1: Yuri Gagarin made one orbit on April 12, 1961. He ejected and parachuted down separately from his capsule.
Human spaceflights by duration.Glenn's Friendship 7: John Glenn orbited Earth three times in 1962. At age 77 he returned to space on the Space Shuttle.
Human spaceflights by duration.Tereshkova's Vostok 6: Valentina Tereshkova orbited 48 times, and remains the only woman to fly a solo space mission.
Human spaceflights by duration.Apollo 11: Armstrong and Aldrin spent about 21 hours on the Moon, around 2.5 outside, while Collins orbited alone.
Human spaceflights by duration.Gemini 7: Frank Borman and Jim Lovell spent two weeks aloft and met Gemini 6A in orbit, proving rendezvous would work.
Human spaceflights by duration.Skylab 4: The last crew to live on Skylab, America's first space station, in 1973 and 1974. The station fell to Earth in 1979.
Human spaceflights by duration.Scott Kelly's 'year': NASA's astronaut Scott Kelly spent a year on the ISS while his identical twin Mark stayed home for genetic comparisons.
Human spaceflights by duration.Frank Rubio's stay: A Soyuz coolant leak extended his stay, making him NASA's record holder for longest single spaceflight in 2023.
Human spaceflights by duration.Valeri Polyakov's stay: The physician Valeri Polyakov lived on Mir for about 438 days in 1994-95, a record that still stands.

European capitals from north to south.Helsinki: Helsinki is a Baltic port founded in 1550 by Sweden's king Gustav I. It is among the world's most northerly capitals, with very long summer days.
European capitals from north to south.Stockholm: Stockholm is built across 14 islands where Lake Mälaren meets the Baltic. The Nobel Prizes, except the peace prize, are awarded here.
European capitals from north to south.Riga: Riga has one of the world's largest collections of Art Nouveau buildings. Its old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
European capitals from north to south.Berlin: Berlin has more bridges than Venice, by some counts. Once divided by a wall, it's now Germany's capital and its largest city.
European capitals from north to south.Prague: Prague's astronomical clock, from 1410, is still working. The city's old centre survived World War II largely intact.
European capitals from north to south.Vienna: Vienna produces wine within its city limits, with vineyards on the edge of town. It has long been a world capital of classical music.
European capitals from north to south.Belgrade: Belgrade sits where the Sava river meets the Danube. It is one of Europe's oldest continuously inhabited cities, with a history of many conquests.
European capitals from north to south.Madrid: At around 650 metres above sea level, Madrid is the highest capital in the EU. Its Prado museum holds works by Goya and Velázquez.
European capitals from north to south.Athens: Named for the goddess Athena, Athens is where democracy began, over 2,500 years ago. The Parthenon still crowns its Acropolis.
European capitals from north to south.Valletta: Valletta is the EU's smallest capital, built by the Knights of St John after the Great Siege of 1565. The whole city is a UNESCO site.

Poker hands, from rarest to most common.Royal flush: Ace-high straight in a single suit; with 52 cards, only four such hands exist, so most players never see one.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.Straight flush: Five consecutive cards of one suit; only 36 such hands exist if you leave out the four royal flushes.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.Four of a kind: Also called quads; 624 hands exist, and if two players hold them, the higher rank of the four wins.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.Full house: Three of one rank plus a pair; when two full houses meet, the higher three-of-a-kind wins, not the higher pair.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.Flush: A flush beats a straight because it is rarer; five same-suit cards turn up about once in 509 deals.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.Straight: The ace may play high or low, so A-2-3-4-5, nicknamed the wheel, is the lowest straight and still beats three of a kind.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.Three of a kind: With two of the three in your own hand it is called a set, and a hidden set is a classic trap for opponents.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.Two pair: Ranked by its higher pair first, then the lower pair, then the leftover fifth card, called the kicker.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.One pair: This is the commonest made hand, and pairs show up in about 42 percent of five-card deals.
Poker hands, from rarest to most common.High card: Nothing matches, so the single highest card decides; this fate befalls roughly half of all five-card hands.

How wide is the target.Golf hole: A golf hole's 4.25-inch width is reputedly based on the pipe once used to cut holes at Musselburgh, Scotland.
How wide is the target.Netball ring: Netball has no backboard, so the ring sticks out from the post, and it's a surprisingly small target.
How wide is the target.Basketball rim: At 18 inches the rim is wide enough for nearly two basketballs side by side.
How wide is the target.Archery target face: The 122 cm face is used at 70 m in the Olympics, and its gold center is only about 12 cm wide.
How wide is the target.Ice hockey goal: Standard goals are six feet wide and four feet high, and the goalie's pads cover much of that.
How wide is the target.Handball goal: Goalkeepers face shots that can top 100 km/h in a goal 3 m wide and 2 m high.
How wide is the target.Field hockey goal: The goal is four yards wide, and a shot in the circle is tricky for a ball just 7 cm across.
How wide is the target.Rugby union posts: Kickers must send the ball between the posts and above a crossbar 3 m off the ground.
How wide is the target.Gaelic football goal: The goalposts are H-shaped: a goal under the bar is worth three points, one over it, one.
How wide is the target.Soccer goal: The goal has been eight yards wide since the 19th century, and the crossbar sits 2.44 m above the ground.

How honey is made, step by step.Bee finds a flower: Scout bees find flowers by colour and scent, and bees can see ultraviolet patterns on petals that guide them to the nectar.
How honey is made, step by step.Bee sips the nectar: The bee sucks nectar through a tongue called a proboscis into a special honey stomach. Collecting enough for a single jar takes many thousands of trips.
How honey is made, step by step.Flies back to the hive: A forager may fly several kilometres and carry nectar about half her body weight. A waggle dance in the hive tells others where to go.
How honey is made, step by step.Passes nectar to a house bee: Foragers hand over nectar mouth to mouth, and house bees pass it on further. The process starts the change from watery nectar into honey.
How honey is made, step by step.House bee adds enzymes: Enzymes break the nectar's complex sugars into simpler ones, which helps honey keep for a very long time. Sealed honey found in Egyptian tombs was still edible.
How honey is made, step by step.Nectar goes into a wax cell: The hexagonal cells are built from wax that bees secrete from their own bodies. Hexagons pack together with no wasted space.
How honey is made, step by step.Bees fan it with their wings: Fanning evaporates water from the nectar, thickening it until it is about 17 to 18 per cent water. That low moisture is what stops it from fermenting.
How honey is made, step by step.Cell is capped with wax: The bees seal ripe honey under a wax lid to preserve it. This stored food gets the colony through winter when no flowers bloom.
How honey is made, step by step.Beekeeper lifts out the frame: Modern hives use removable frames, an idea patented by Lorenzo Langstroth in 1852. A good frame can hold a few kilograms of honey.
How honey is made, step by step.Honey is spun out and jarred: An extractor spins the frames so honey flies out by centrifugal force, leaving the comb undamaged to be reused by the bees.

Hansel and Gretel, in story order.Famine strikes the family: Some historians link the story's abandoned children to the Great Famine of the early 1300s.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.Hansel drops white pebbles: White pebbles shine in the moonlight, a clever trail, and the Grimms' 1812 tale gives Hansel the early plan.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.They find their way home: In the earliest Grimm editions the villain is the children's own mother; later versions made her a stepmother.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.Led into the woods again: The second time, Hansel cannot collect pebbles because the door is locked, so he has to use bread.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.Birds eat the breadcrumbs: Birds eating the trail made breadcrumbs a byword; today a breadcrumb trail is also a website's navigation links.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.They find a gingerbread house: Gingerbread houses are said to have become a German Christmas tradition after the Grimms' tale spread.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.The witch locks up Hansel: The witch has poor eyesight, which sets up the trick that keeps Hansel alive.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.Hansel holds out a bone: Hansel sticks out a bone for the nearly blind witch to feel, making her think he is still too thin to eat.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.Gretel shoves the witch inside: Humperdinck's 1893 opera Hänsel und Gretel brought the story to the stage and is still performed at Christmas.
Hansel and Gretel, in story order.Home again with jewels: The witch's jewels make the family rich, and in the Grimms' version the cruel stepmother has died by the time they return.

Star Wars films, by release year.A New Hope: Originally titled just Star Wars, the Episode IV label was added when the film was rereleased.
Star Wars films, by release year.The Empire Strikes Back: The I am your father twist was kept so secret that on set the line David Prowse spoke was different.
Star Wars films, by release year.Return of the Jedi: The forest moon scenes with the Ewoks were filmed in California's redwood forests.
Star Wars films, by release year.The Phantom Menace: It arrived after a sixteen-year gap and introduced Jar Jar Binks, with groundbreaking CGI.
Star Wars films, by release year.Attack of the Clones: It was the first major film shot entirely on high-definition digital cameras.
Star Wars films, by release year.Revenge of the Sith: The darkest film in the series, it was the first Star Wars film to get a PG-13 rating.
Star Wars films, by release year.The Force Awakens: It earned over two billion dollars and was the biggest US box-office hit at the time.
Star Wars films, by release year.Rogue One: A standalone story about stealing the Death Star plans, its ending leads directly into A New Hope.
Star Wars films, by release year.The Last Jedi: It was the last film Carrie Fisher completed, as Leia; she died in December 2016 before its release.
Star Wars films, by release year.Solo: It tells Han Solo's origin story, including the Kessel Run in under twelve parsecs.

Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Black-footed cat: Africa's smallest cat has one of the highest hunt success rates, reportedly killing about 60 percent of its attacks, hunting at night.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Sand cat: It lives in deserts, with fur-covered paw pads that insulate from hot sand, and survives on little water.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Domestic cat: Domestication began around 10,000 years ago, when cats likely joined farmers to hunt rodents.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Serval: Its long legs and big ears help it leap about three metres high to catch birds.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Eurasian lynx: The largest lynx has tufted ears and a short tail; it lives silently in northern forests and has been reintroduced to parts of Europe.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Cheetah: The fastest land animal sprints at up to about 100 km/h, but cannot roar and purrs instead.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Cougar: Also called puma or mountain lion, it holds a record for having the most names of any animal.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Jaguar: It has the strongest bite relative to size among big cats, capable of piercing turtle shells and skulls.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Lion: The only cat living in groups, called prides; a male's mane signals his health.
Wild and domestic cats, by weight.Siberian tiger: The largest cat, also called the Amur tiger; each tiger's stripes are unique.

Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Cucumber: Cucumbers are about 95 percent water, which is why they offer so little protein and make an excellent hydrating snack.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Potato: Potatoes have little protein, but they're a notable source of vitamin C and potassium, and were once a staple that fed whole nations.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Quinoa (cooked): Technically a seed, quinoa is a rare plant that supplies all nine essential amino acids, and the Incas called it the 'mother grain'.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Lentils (cooked): Among the oldest cultivated crops, lentils have been farmed for roughly nine thousand years and are a staple across South Asia.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Edamame: These are simply young soybeans picked before they harden, and they're a complete protein, rare for a plant.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Tempeh: Fermenting soybeans with a mold makes this Indonesian food firm and nutty, and fermenting makes its nutrients easier to absorb.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Almonds: Botanically the seed of a fruit related to peaches, almonds are also a good source of vitamin E and healthy fats.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Peanuts: Despite the name, peanuts are legumes that grow underground, making them kin to lentils and beans rather than tree nuts.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Hemp seeds: These seeds are a complete protein and a source of omega-3 fats, and they contain virtually none of the psychoactive compounds in cannabis.
Protein per 100 g in plant foods.Spirulina (dried): This blue-green microorganism was eaten by the Aztecs, and today it's sold as a supplement because its dried weight is over half protein.
